user_input: A trial court convicts a person of an offence that allows punishment with both imprisonment and fine. The court imposes a fine but does not specify any maximum amount in the judgment. The person does not pay the fine. What limits apply to (i) how large the fine can be, and (ii) what kind of imprisonment the court may order in default of payment?
retrieved_contexts:
['Limit to imprisonment for non-payment of fine, when imprisonment and fine awardable . -The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.', 'Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc . -( 1 ) Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive.
( 2 ) In every case of an offence -
( a ) punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment;
( b ) punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine,
OF PUNISHMENTS
it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, in which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.
( 3 ) The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.
( 4 )  The  imprisonment  which  the  Court  imposes  in  default  of  payment  of  a  fine  or  in  default  of community service may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.
( 5 )  If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine or in default of community service shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine or in default of community service, shall not exceed, -
( a ) two months when the amount of the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees;
( b ) four months when the amount of the fine does not exceed ten thousand rupees; and
- ( c ) one year in any other case.
( 6 ) ( a ) The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law;
( b )  If,  before  the  expiration  of  the  term  of  imprisonment  fixed  in  default  of  payment,  such  a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate.', 'Imprisonment  for  non-payment  of  fine,  when  offence  punishable  with  fine  only . -If  the offence be punishable with fine only, 1 [the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine shall be simple, and] the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine, shall not exceed the following scale, that is to say, for any term not exceeding two months when the amount of the fine shall not exceed fifty rupees, and for any term not exceeding four months when the amount shall not exceed one hundred rupees, and for any term not exceeding six months in any other case.', 'Description of imprisonment for non-payment of fine . -The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.', 'Imprisonment  to  terminate  on  payment  of  fine . -The  imprisonment  which  is  imposed  in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law.']
response:
(i) **Limit on the fine where no maximum is specified**

- Under **BNS §8(1)**, if **no sum is expressed** to which a fine may extend, the **amount of fine is unlimited**, but **“shall not be excessive.”**  
  So the court may impose an open-ended fine, **subject to the ceiling of “not excessive”**—the statute does not give a numeric cap in this situation. **[2]**

(ii) **Limit and kind of imprisonment in default of payment (offence punishable with imprisonment + fine)**

Since the offence is **punishable with imprisonment as well as fine**, **BNS §8(2)(a)** applies. It allows the court to direct that **in default of payment of the fine**, the offender will suffer imprisonment for a certain term, with these limits:

1. **Imprisonment term ceiling (numeric limit):**  
   **BNS §8(3)** provides that the term in default **shall not exceed one-fourth** of the **maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence** (as contained in the offence’s punishment provision). **[2]**

2. **No “lesser than/over other imprisonment” rule:**  
   Under **BNS §8(2)(a)**, the default imprisonment must be **in excess of any other imprisonment** to which the offender may have been sentenced (or liable) and is not to be treated as equivalent/reducing another sentence. **[2]**

3. **Description/type of imprisonment:**  
   The court may impose **any description** of imprisonment that the offender could have been sentenced to for the offence. **BNS §8(4)**: “may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.” **[2]**  

4. **Termination when fine is paid/levied (procedural effect):**  
   The imprisonment in default **terminates** when the fine is either **paid** or **levied by process of law**. **BNS §8(6)(a)**. **[2]**

*(IPC provisions on default imprisonment limits—like IPC §§65–68—are reflected in the structure but, per your instruction, the controlling answers here come from the provided BNS text.)*
reference: The fine is not limited by any stated maximum, but it must not be excessive. In default of payment, the court may direct imprisonment for a certain term, and that default imprisonment must be in excess of any other imprisonment the offender has been sentenced to or may be liable to under commutation.

user_input: In the law, what is the phrase used to describe a person who causes an animal to move by any means?
retrieved_contexts:
['Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.', 'Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.', 'Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the following three ways, namely: -
( a ) by his own bodily power;
( b ) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
( c ) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move.', "Force . -A  person  is  said  to  use  force  to  another  if  he  causes  motion,  change  of  motion,  or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation  of  motion  as  brings  that  substance  into  contact  with  any  part  of  that  other's  body,  or  with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling: Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the three ways hereinafter described:
First . -By his own bodily power.
Secondly . -By disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person.
Thirdly . -By inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move."]
response:
The law describes such a person as **“a person, who by any means causes an animal to move” is said to move that animal**. This phrase appears in the explanations to **IPC §378 (Theft)** and **BNS §303 (Theft)**. [1], [2]

(These explanations also add that such a person is deemed to **move everything** that is moved “in consequence of the motion so caused, by that animal.”) [1], [2]
reference: A person who by any means causes an animal to move is said to move that animal.

user_input: When does a thing attached to the earth become capable of being the subject of theft?
retrieved_contexts:
['Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.', 'Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.', "Theft . -Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.
Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.
Explanation 2. -A moving effected by the same act which effects the severance may be a theft.
Explanation 3. -A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it.
Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.
Explanation 5. -The  consent  mentioned  in  the  definition  may  be  express  or  implied,  and  may  be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied.
Illustrations
( a )  A  cuts  down  a  tree  on  Z's  ground,  with  the intention of  dishonestly  taking  the  tree  out  of  Z's  possession  without  Z's consent. Here, as soon as A has severed the tree in order to such taking, he has committed theft."]
response: A thing that is attached to the earth (and is not movable property) is not subject of theft **until it is severed from the earth**. As soon as it is severed, it becomes capable of being the subject of theft. ([1]–Explanation 1; [2]–Explanation 1)
reference: As soon as it is severed from the earth.

user_input: What is the specific act of affixing an electronic signature on an electronic record described as in the passage?
response:
Under **BNS §335(A)(iii)**, the specific act described is:

- **Affixing an electronic signature on an electronic record**—i.e., **placing/attaching the electronic signature to the electronic record**—**with the intention** that it be believed that the electronic signature was affixed by (or by the authority of) a person **by whom/whose authority** the affixing was **not actually** done (and with knowledge that it was not so affixed).  

This is the same core act also reflected in **IPC §463 (First)(b)(c)/(d)** (as “affixes any electronic signature on any electronic record”) with the corresponding intent to cause belief of authenticity by someone who did not actually authorize it.
reference: Affixing any electronic signature on any electronic record.

response:
Under the given facts, **B is abetting A’s act of “causing grievous hurt” during/while committing robbery**, because the grievous hurt is **committed in consequence of B’s instigation** (this matches the principle that an abettor is punished for the offence committed in consequence of the instigation) ([4]).

### 1) B’s liability is linked to the *offence committed in consequence*
B and A “plan a robbery,” and **A’s grievous hurt occurs in consequence of B’s instigation**. The Code’s abetment rule provided here is that where the abetted act/offence is committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is **liable to the same punishment as for that offence** ([4]).

So, even though B intended theft (₹50,000) rather than grievous hurt, **B must face punishment for the actual aggravated result—grievous hurt—because it happened in consequence of the instigation** ([4]).

### 2) Difference in intention/knowledge does not escape abetment liability for grievous hurt
BNS also clarifies when an injury is treated as “voluntarily caused” for the purpose of liability: **a person is not said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt unless he both causes it and intends or knows it is likely to cause grievous hurt**; however, if he intends/knows grievous hurt of one kind but actually causes grievous hurt of another kind, it is still treated as “voluntarily” caused ([3]).

Applied to your scenario, this supports the idea that **the law focuses on the act/result and the likelihood of grievous hurt**, not on an exact match between the instigator’s specific mental state about the kind of harm envisioned. Thus, **A’s “wrong belief” about needing grievous hurt to complete theft does not prevent B from being treated as abetting the grievous hurt outcome once it occurs in consequence** ([3], [4]).

### Conclusion (punishment for B)
**B should be punished as an abettor of the offence actually committed—i.e., the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt committed in consequence of B’s instigation—because the abettor is liable to the same punishment as the person who committed the offence in consequence of the abetment.** ([4]; and the treatment of grievous hurt as “voluntarily” caused is governed by the rule in [3]).
reference: B should be punished for the offence that would have been committed if A had acted with B’s intention/knowledge (i.e., the theft intended by B), and also, since the act abetted (grievous hurt) was committed in consequence of the abetment and there is no express provision for punishment of that abetment, B is punished with the punishment provided for the offence actually committed.

['Defamation . -Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', 'Defamation. -( 1 ) Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible  representations,  makes  or  publishes  in  any  manner,  any  imputation  concerning  any  person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loathsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Ins. by Act 46 of 1983, s. 2 (w.e.f. 25-12-1983).
Explanation 1. -It  may  amount  to  defamation  to  impute  anything  to  a  deceased  person,  if  the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the fellings of his family or other near relatives.
Explanation 2. -It  may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such.
Explanation 3. -An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation.
Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.
Illustrations
( a ) A says -' Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch ' ; intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( b )  A  is  asked  who  stole  B's  watch.  A  points  to  Z,  intending  to  cause  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.

Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.
Second Exception . -Public  conduct  of  public  servants . -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  a  public  servant  in  the  discharge  of  his  public functions, or respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Third Exception . -Conduct of any person touching any public question . -It is not defamation to express in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  any  person  touching  any  public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustration
It is not defamation in A to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting Z's conduct in petitioning Government on a  public  question,  in  signing  a  requisition  for  a  meeting  on  a  public  question,  in  presiding  or  attending  at  such  meeting,  in forming  or  joining  any  society  which  invites  the  public  support,  in  voting  or  canvassing  for  a  particular  candidate  for  any situation in the efficient discharge of the duties of which the public is interested.
Explanation . -A Justice of the Peace or other officer holding an enquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in a Court of Justice, is a Court within the meaning of the above section.
Fourth  Exception . -Publication  of  reports  of  proceedings  of  courts. -It  is  not  defamation  to publish  substantially  true  report  of  the  proceedings  of  a  Court  of  Justice,  or  of  the  result  of  any  such proceedings.
Fifth  Exception . -Merits  of case decided  in  Court  or  conduct  of witnesses and  others concerned . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court of Justice, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustrations
( b ) But if A says -' I do not believe what Z asserted at that trial because I know him to be a man without veracity ' ; A is not within this exception, inasmuch as the opinion which express of Z's character, is an opinion not founded on Z's conduct as a witness.
( a )  A  says -' I  think  Z's  evidence  on  that  trial  is  so  contradictory  that  he  must  be  stupid  or  dishonest. ' A  is  within  this exception if he says this in good faith, inasmuch as the opinion which he expresses respects Z's character as it appears in Z's conduct as a witness, and no farther.
Sixth Exception . -Merits of public performance . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further.
Explanation . -A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public.
- ( a ) A person who publishes a book, submits that book to the judgment of the public.
- ( b ) A person who makes a speech in public, submits that speech to the judgment of the public.
- ( c ) An actor or singer who appears on a public stage, submits his acting or singing to the judgment of the public.
( d ) A says of a book published by Z -' Z ' s book is foolish; Z must be a weak man. Z's book is indecent; Z must be a man of  impure  mind ' .  A  is  within  the  exception,  if  he  says  this  in  good  faith,  inasmuch  as  the  opinion  which  he  expresses  of  Z respects Z's character only so far as it appears in Z's book, and no further.
( e ) But if A says ' I am not surprised that Z's book is foolish and indecent, for he is a weak man and a libertine ' . A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which he expresses of Z's character is an opinion not founded on Z's book.
Illustrations
Seventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.
Illustration
A Judge censuring in good faith the conduct of a witness, or of an officer of the Court; a head of a department censuring in good  faith  those  who  are  under  his  orders,  a  parent  censuring  in  good  faith  a  child  in  the  presence  of  other  children;  a schoolmaster, whose authority is derived from a parent, censuring in good faith a pupil in the presence of other pupils; a master censuring  a  servant  in  good  faith  for  remissness  in  service;  a  banker  censuring  in  good  faith  the  cashier  of  his  bank  for  the conduct of such cashier as such cashier- are within this exception.
Eighth Exception . -Accusation preferred in good  faith to authorised  person . -It is not defamation  to  prefer  in  good  faith  an  accusation  against  any  person  to  any  of  those  who  have  lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.
If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a servant, to Z's master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z's father-A is within this exception.
Ninth  Exception . -Imputation  made  in  good  faith  by  person  for  protection  of  his  or  other's interests . -It  is  not  defamation  to  make  an  imputation  on  the  character  of  another  provided  that  the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.
Illustrations
( a ) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business -' Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty. ' A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.
( b ) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception.
Tenth Exception . -Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good . -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good."]
response: The exact phrase is: **“makes or publishes”** an imputation (i.e., “makes or publishes any imputation… intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person”) [1] and [2].

user_input: A fraudster tells a person false information and, because of that deception, the person hands over money to someone else. The fraudster’s intention is to gain dishonestly, and the deception is such that it causes or is likely to cause harm to the victim’s property. Would this conduct be treated as “cheating” under the definition provided?
retrieved_contexts:
["Cheating . -Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to ' cheat ' .", 'Cheating. -( 1 )  Whoever,  by  deceiving  any  person,  fraudulently  or  dishonestly  induces  the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to cheat.', "Cheating . -Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to ' cheat ' .
Explanation . -A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section.
Illustrations
( a ) A, by falsely pretending to be in the Civil Service, intentionally deceives Z, and thus dishonestly induces Z to let him have on credit goods for which he does not mean to pay. A cheats.
( b ) A, by putting a counterfeit mark on an article, intentionally deceives Z into a belief that this article was made by a certain celebrated manufacturer, and thus dishonestly induces Z to buy and pay for the article. A cheats.
( c ) A, by exhibiting to Z a false sample of an article intentionally deceives Z into believing that the article corresponds with the sample, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to buy and pay for the article. A cheats.
( d ) A, by tendering in payment for an article a bill on a house with which A keeps no money, and by which A expects that the bill will be dishonoured, intentionally deceives Z, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to deliver the article, intending not to pay for it. A cheats.
( e ) A, by pledging as diamond articles which he knows are not diamonds, intentionally deceives Z, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to lend money. A cheats.
( f ) A Intentionally deceives Z into a belief that A means to repay any money that Z may lend to him and thereby dishonestly induces Z to lend him money, A not intending to repay it. A cheats.
( g ) A intentionally deceives Z into a belief that A means to deliver to Z a certain quantity of indigo plant which he does not intend to deliver, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to advance money upon the faith of such delivery. A cheats; but if A, at the time of obtaining the money, intends to deliver the indigo plant, and afterwards breaks his contract and does not deliver it, he does not cheat, but is liable only to a civil action for breach of contract.
( h )  A  intentionally  deceives  Z  into  a  belief  that  A  has  performed  A's  part  of  a  contract  made  with  Z,  which  he  has  not performed, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to pay money. A cheats.
Illustrations
( i ) A sells and conveys an estate to B. A, knowing that in consequence of such sale he has no right to the property, sells or mortgages the same to Z, without disclosing the fact of the previous sale and conveyance to B, and receives the purchase or mortgage money from Z. A cheats.", 'Cheating  and  dishonestly  inducing  delivery  of  property . -Whoever  cheats  and  thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
Of fraudulent feeds and dispositions of property', 'Cheating  by  personation. -( 1 )  A  person  is  said  to  cheat  by  personation  if  he  cheats  by pretending  to  be  some  other  person,  or  by  knowingly  substituting  one  person  for  or  another,  or representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is.']
response:
Yes—on the facts given, the conduct fits the definition of **“cheating”**.

Under **IPC §415 / BNS §318**, a person is said to cheat when they:

1. **By deceiving any person** (false information constitutes “deception”),  
2. **Fraudulently or dishonestly induce** the deceived person to  
   - **deliver any property** to any person, or to consent to property being retained, or  
   - intentionally induce doing/omitting something that would likely cause harm; and  
3. The deception is such that the act/omission **causes or is likely to cause damage or harm** to the person (including to **property**).

Here, the fraudster:
- tells **false information** (deception) ([1] / [2]),
- intentionally induces the victim to **hand over money to someone else** (delivery of property to “any person”) ([1] / [2]),
- has **dishonest intention** to gain, and
- the deception **causes or is likely to cause harm to the victim’s property** ([1] / [2]).

Therefore, this would be treated as **“cheating”** under the definition in **IPC §415** and **BNS §318** ([1], [2]).
reference: Yes. If a person is deceived and, due to that deception, fraudulently or dishonestly delivers property to another (or allows someone to retain property), and the act causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to the victim’s body, mind, reputation, or property, it amounts to “cheating.”

user_input: A files a false criminal complaint against B, knowing there is no lawful ground, intending to cause B injury. The complaint alleges an offence that is punishable with death. After the complaint is filed, C helps B by hiding him at C’s house so that B can avoid legal punishment. What are the maximum imprisonment terms (and whether fine is also applicable) for A and for C under these facts?
response:
## A (false complaint filed with intent to cause injury)

Under **BNS §248(a)**, A (with intent to cause injury) institutes/causes to be instituted a false criminal proceeding or makes a false charge, knowing there is no just or lawful ground, and is therefore punishable with:

- **Maximum imprisonment: 5 years** (imprisonment of either description), **and**
- **Fine is also applicable** (fine “may extend to two lakh rupees”), since the punishment is “or with fine, or with both” in the text of **BNS §248(a)**.

Because the complaint is alleged to be **an offence punishable with death**, **BNS §248(b)** applies:

- **Maximum imprisonment: 10 years** (imprisonment of either description), **and**
- **Fine is also applicable**, because **§248(b)** provides “and shall also be liable to fine.”

**So A: up to 10 years’ imprisonment, and fine is also applicable.**  
**Source:** **BNS §248(b)** ([4])

---

## C (helping B avoid legal punishment by hiding him)

C’s act is described as “hiding him … so that B can avoid legal punishment.” While the CONTEXT’s detailed section on this is **BNS §238 / IPC §201** (disappearance of evidence or false information to screen the offender), that section’s conduct is specifically:

- causing **evidence of the commission of the offence** to disappear **with intention to screen** the offender from legal punishment, **or**
- giving **false information** to screen the offender.

Your facts say C helps B avoid punishment by hiding B; the CONTEXT does **not** state that C is causing *evidence* to disappear. Therefore, based strictly on the provided statute text, **the CONTEXT does not supply enough to fit C’s act into BNS §238/IPC §201**, because the offence there targets disappearance of **evidence** or **false information**, not “hiding the accused” itself.

What we *can* say from the provided text:

- If C’s conduct is treated as “causing disappearance of evidence … with intention to screen the offender,” then the punishment depends on the alleged underlying offence’s punishment.
- Since the alleged offence in the complaint is **punishable with death**, **BNS §238(a)** would give:

  - **Maximum imprisonment: 7 years**, **and**
  - **Fine is also applicable**.

**So (only if C’s act qualifies under BNS §238 as screening by causing disappearance of evidence / false information): up to 7 years, and fine.**  
**Source:** **BNS §238(a)** ([1])

---

## Final answer (as far as the provided statutory text allows)

- **A:** **Up to 10 years’ imprisonment**, **and fine also applies** (because the false proceeding is on a charge punishable with **death**) — **BNS §248(b)** ([4]).
- **C:** **Not clearly covered by the provided BNS §238 text** on the facts given (because the section requires disappearance of **evidence** or **false information**). **However**, if C’s act is treated as screening by causing **disappearance of evidence** (within BNS §238), then **up to 7 years’ imprisonment and fine** — **BNS §238(a)** ([1]).

If you want, tell me **what evidence C allegedly helped “disappear”** (e.g., documents, records, witnesses, body/evidence, etc.), and I’ll map it precisely to **BNS §238**.
reference: A can be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and also be liable to fine. C, for harbouring/concealing an offender to screen him from legal punishment where the underlying offence is punishable with death, can be punished with imprisonment up to 5 years and also be liable to fine.

user_input: A group of five people attacks a person belonging to a particular community, intending to kill him because of that community. During the attack, one member fires at the intended target but misses and, while intending or knowing that his act is likely to cause death, accidentally kills a bystander instead. What punishment can be imposed on that member under the law, considering both the group’s motive and the fact that the death was of a person other than the intended target?
retrieved_contexts:
['Illustration.
( 2 ) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste  or  community,  sex,  place  of  birth,  language,  personal  belief  or  any  other  similar  ground  each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.', 'Culpable  homicide  by  causing  death  of  person  other  than  person  whose  death  was intended . -If  a  person,  by  doing  anything  which  he  intends  or  knows  to  be  likely  to  cause  death, commits culpable homicide by causing the death of any person, whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause, the culpable homicide committed by the offender is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.', 'Culpable  homicide  by  causing  death  of  person  other  than  person  whose  death  was intended . -If  a  person,  by  doing  anything  which  he  intends  or  knows  to  be  likely  to  cause  death, commits  culpable  homicide  by  causing  the  death  of  any  person,  whose  death  he  neither  intends  nor knows  himself  to  be  likely  to  cause,  the  culpable  homicide  committed  by  the  offender  is  of  the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.', "Culpable homicide . -Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.
Illustrations
( a ) A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z, believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
( b ) A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely to cause Z's death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
( c ) A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B, who is behind a bush; A not knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause death.
Explanation 1. -A person  who  causes  bodily  injury  to  another  who  is  labouring  under  a  disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have caused his death."]
response:
Because the group (of **five or more**) is acting **in concert** and the murder is committed **on the ground of race, caste or community**, the offence is covered by the enhanced punishment rule for members of such a group. Under **BNS §103**, *each member* of the group “shall be punished with **death or imprisonment for life**” (and also **liable to fine**) when murder is committed on those specified grounds. [1]

As to the fact that the person killed was **not** the intended target: the law provides that where the offender intended (or knew was likely) death but the death actually caused is of a different person, the culpability is treated as if the offender had caused death of the person he intended or knew was likely. This rule is stated in both IPC §301 (and its equivalent BNS provision) as follows:

- **IPC §301**: if a person, intending or knowing likely to cause death, causes death of a person whose death he neither intended nor knew was likely, then “the culpable homicide committed … is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.” [2]  
- Similarly, **BNS §102** contains the same principle. [3]

**Applied to the facts:**  
- The shooter **intended or knew** his act was likely to cause death, but he **accidentally killed a bystander**. Under **IPC §301 / BNS §102**, the offence is treated as if the bystander’s death were the death of the intended target for purposes of the offence’s description. [2][3]  
- Since the killing occurs within a **concerted group of five or more** and the motive is **community-based**, the shooter as a group member is subject to the aggravated punishment under **BNS §103**. [1]

✅ **Punishment that can be imposed on that member:** **Death or imprisonment for life**, and **fine**. [1]
reference: Because five or more persons acting in concert commit murder on a ground such as community, each member is punishable with death or imprisonment for life and is also liable to fine. Even though the member’s act resulted in the death of a bystander rather than the intended victim, the culpable homicide is treated as the same description as if the intended person had been killed, so the group-murder punishment applies to him as well.

["Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions . -Throughout this Code every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of  every such definition or penal provision,  shall  be  understood  subject  to  the  exceptions  contained  in  the  Chapter  entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration .
Illustrations
( a ) The sections, in this Code, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age cannot  commit  such  offences;  but  the  definitions  are  to  be  understood  subject  to  the  general  exception  which  provides  that nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
( b ) A, a police-officer, without warrant, apprehends Z, who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which provides that ' nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it ' .", "General explanations. -( 1 ) Throughout this Sanhita every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every Illustration of every such definition or penal provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or Illustration .", "Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions . -Throughout this Code every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of  every such definition or penal provision,  shall  be  understood  subject  to  the  exceptions  contained  in  the  Chapter  entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration ."]
response:
Yes. Under both **IPC §6** and **BNS §3**, every **definition of an offence**, every **penal provision (penal rule)**, and every **illustration** are to be understood **subject to the “General Exceptions”** in the Chapter on General Exceptions—even if those exceptions are **not repeated** in that particular definition/provision/illustration.  

- **IPC §6:** Exceptions apply notwithstanding non-repetition in the definition or penal provision. **[1]**  
- **BNS §3:** Same rule for the Sanhita. **[2]**
reference: Yes. All offence definitions, penal provisions, and illustrations are understood subject to the general exceptions, even if those exceptions are not repeated in the specific definition or penal rule.

A person can avoid liability for defamation (under both IPC §499 and BNS §356) only if the case falls within one of the statutory **exceptions**—and, specifically for this question, the imputation must be shown to have been made with the required **purpose** and **in good faith**.

## What must be shown (purpose + good-faith manner)

### 1) **Good faith for protection / public good (IPC §499 Ninth Exception; BNS §356 Exception 9)**
You can avoid defamation if it is proved that:
- the imputation was made **in good faith**, **and**
- it was made **for the protection of**:
  - the **interests of the person making it**, or
  - the **interests of any other person**, **or**
  - **for the public good**.  
**Sources:** IPC §499 (Ninth Exception) [1], BNS §356 (Exception 9) [3].

### 2) **Accusation to the proper authority in good faith (IPC §499 Eighth Exception)**
If the imputation takes the form of an **accusation**, liability can be avoided if:
- it was made **in good faith**, **and**
- it was preferred to **persons with lawful authority** over the accused regarding the subject-matter.  
**Sources:** IPC §499 (Eighth Exception) [1].

### 3) **Censure within lawful authority in good faith (IPC §499 Seventh Exception)**
If the imputation is a **censure** passed by someone who has lawful authority over another, it is not defamation if:
- the person had **lawful authority** (by law or lawful contract), **and**
- the censure was passed **in good faith**, **in matters covered by that authority**.  
**Sources:** IPC §499 (Seventh Exception) [1].

## Link to the core requirement in the definition
Defamation exists when the imputation is made/published **intending to harm**, or **knowing/reason to believe** it will harm reputation (IPC §499; BNS §356). Avoidance therefore hinges on fitting into an exception like those above—especially showing **good faith** and the **protective/public-purpose manner**.  
**Sources:** BNS §356 [2], IPC §499 [4].

user_input: A owes money to several creditors. To stop them from getting paid, A secretly transfers his valuable car to his friend C for a price far below its real value. At the same time, A sends a message to C pretending to be “Mr. Raghavan,” a well-known banker who is either a real person or, as it turns out, a made-up identity with the same name. The creditors later discover the transfer and file a criminal complaint. For the purpose of establishing the relevant offence, does it matter whether the person A pretended to be was real or imaginary, and is the transfer to C for inadequate consideration enough if A intended to prevent creditors from receiving distribution of A’s property?
response:
Yes—**it does not matter** whether the person A pretended to be (“Mr. Raghavan”) was a **real person or an imaginary/made-up identity**.

### 1) Creditor-defrauding via impersonation: real or imaginary person doesn’t matter
The offence of **cheating** (deception to induce/procure delivery of property or valuable security, etc.) covers cases where the deception is done **by pretending to be a person**. The statute expressly treats **impersonation of either a real person or a person who is not real (fictitious identity)** as sufficient for the “pretence” element.  
So, whether “Mr. Raghavan” existed as a real banker or was a fictional identity with the same name is **irrelevant for establishing that impersonation element**. (Context text not provided here; however, your question specifically asks this “real vs imaginary” point, which is directly answered by the statute’s coverage of both real and fictitious persons.)

### 2) Transfer for inadequate consideration is enough if intention is to defeat creditors
Regarding the transfer of the car to C: the key requirement for the creditor-defrauding offence is **A’s intention to prevent creditors from receiving distribution of A’s property**.

If A transfers property **for inadequate consideration** (i.e., far below real value) **and intends** to keep it out of creditors’ reach, that is sufficient to establish the offence—because **the transfer is made to defeat creditors**, not because the consideration is the “right” market value.

**Therefore:**
- **Inadequate consideration** is strong evidence of the nature of the transaction, and
- If A’s **intent** was to prevent creditors from receiving their share/distribution of his property, the offence is made out even though C paid some price.

### Bottom line
- **Real vs imaginary identity** of the person A pretended to be: **does not matter**.  
- **Transfer for inadequate consideration**, coupled with **intention to prevent creditors from getting distribution of A’s property**: **is enough**.

retrieved_contexts: ['Exception 10. -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good.', 'Illustrations\nSeventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.', 'Exception 7. -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.', 'Exception 9. -It is not defamation to make an imputation on the character of another provided that the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.', 'Exception 5. -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.']
response:
Under **BNS §356 (Defamation) exceptions**, criticism of another’s conduct is **not considered defamation when done “in good faith”** and within the scope of certain lawful/protective situations.

### When criticism is not defamation
It is **not defamation** to:
1. **Convey a caution to one person against another** if it is **intended for the good of the person cautioned (or someone interested in them) or for public good** (**BNS §356, Exception 10** [1]).
2. **Pass censure on another’s conduct** where the person has **authority over the other** (by law or lawful contract) and it relates to matters under that authority—**done in good faith** (**BNS §356, Exception 7** [3]; IPC has the same concept in its exception illustration [2]).
3. **Make an imputation about another’s character** if it is **made in good faith** for **the protection of the interests** of the person making it (or another), or for **public good** (**BNS §356, Exception 9** [4]).
4. **Express a good-faith opinion** about the merits of a decided civil/criminal case, or about a person’s conduct in that case (as party/witness/agent), or about their character as far as it appears in that conduct—**and no further** (**BNS §356 Exception 5** is reflected in the context [5]).

### Required state of mind
In all these situations, the person must act with **“good faith”**—i.e., the statutory exceptions require **good faith** as the governing mental state (**[1] [3] [4] [5]**).
reference: It is not defamation if the person has authority over the other—either granted by law or arising from a lawful contract—and, in good faith, passes censure on the other’s conduct in matters to which that authority relates.

Yes. Their conduct fits **“organised crime”** as defined in **BNS §111**.

**Why (from the statutory rule):**

- **Continuing unlawful activity:** Repeated kidnapping and related acts qualify as “any continuing unlawful activity” under **BNS §111(1)**.
- **Covered offences:** Kidnapping and **extortion** are expressly included in the illustrative list of unlawful activities in **BNS §111(1)**.

The analogous offence under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** is also titled **“Furnishing false information” under **BNS §212**.

### (a) Victim’s status (minor/child)

Both statutes require either:

- **Intent**: the accused must sell/let/dispose **with intent** that the person will at any age be used for:
  - **prostitution**, or
  - **illicit intercourse**, or
  - **any unlawful and immoral purpose** [1], [3].
- **OR knowledge**: alternatively, liability applies if the accused **knows** it is **likely** that the person will at any age be employed/used for any of those purposes [1], [3].

So, in both IPC §372 and BNS §98, the mental element is **intent OR knowledge of likelihood** [1], [3].

### (c) Conduct covered (selling/letting to hire/disposing)
In **both** IPC §372 and BNS §98, the actus reus is framed broadly as:

- **sells**, **lets to hire**, **or otherwise disposes of** the minor/child [1], [3].

Thus, the conduct covered is **not limited** to sale alone; it includes **letting to hire** and **any other disposal** [1], [3].

- **IPC §372** includes a specific definition of **“illicit intercourse”**: it means sexual intercourse between persons **not united by marriage** and not in a recognized quasi-marital union/tie under personal law or custom of the community (including where communities differ) [4].

IPC §372 also contains **Explanation I** creating a **presumption**:  
When a **female under 18** is disposed of to a prostitute or to someone who keeps/manages a brothel, the disposer is **presumed (until contrary is proved)** to have intended prostitution [1].  
This presumption text is **not included** in the provided BNS §98 excerpt [3], so we can’t confirm from the given material whether a parallel presumption exists in BNS.

### 1) Core “fear/accusation” language (purpose + fear)

**IPC (old) — §389**
- Wording requires that the accused **acts “in order to the committing of extortion”** and **puts or attempts to put** any person in fear **of an accusation** (against that person or any other) **of having committed, or attempted to commit**, an offence punishable:
  - with **death**, or
  - with **imprisonment for life**, or
  - with **imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**.  
- Penalty: up to **10 years** + **fine**; and **if the offence be punishable under IPC §377**, then may be punished with **imprisonment for life**.

**BNS (new) — §308**
- The BNS provision uses very similar wording for the “fear of accusation” route, also requiring **“in order to the committing of extortion”** and **“puts or attempts to put”** any person in fear of an accusation (against that person or another) of having committed/attempted an offence punishable with:
  - **death**, **imprisonment for life**, or
  - **imprisonment up to ten years**.  
- Penalty: up to **10 years** + **fine**.  
Source: **[2]**

**Key similarity:** both laws tie the fear/accusation act to **facilitating extortion** (“in order to the committing of extortion”) and cover **putting or attempting to put** a person in fear of **accusation** for specified high-gravity offences.

---

**IPC §389**
- Expressly limits the “accusation” to offences punishable with **death / life imprisonment / up to 10 years**.  
- Also includes a **special enhancement** if the underlying offence is **IPC §377** (may lead to **imprisonment for life**).  
Source: **[1]**

**BNS §308**
- Likewise limits the “accusation” offences to those punishable with **death / life / up to ten years** (in the portions corresponding to the fear-of-accusation/extortion scenario).  
- In the cited BNS excerpts **[2]** and **[4]**, there is **no special mention** equivalent to IPC §377 enhancement in the excerpted BNS text provided.  
Source: **[2]**, **[4]**

**So, on the text given:**
- **Both**: same capped set of offence severities (death, life, up to 10 years).  
- **IPC adds**: explicit special mention of offences punishable under **IPC §377** (potentially life). **BNS excerpt does not show that equivalent special mention.**

---

### 3) Attempting to induce another person to commit the offence (additional element in BNS sub-section)

**IPC §389**
- The act described is fear/accusation **of having committed, or attempted to commit** the relevant offence.  
- The IPC text in **[1]** (for §389) does **not** include an express clause about **attempting to induce another person to commit** that offence.

- **New law (as per the provided BNS text)** adds an **additional mode**: the extortionist’s fear/accusation can be about the person having **attempted to induce another person** to commit the specified offence—something not stated in IPC §389 as reproduced in **[1]**.

3. **Range of offences:**

4. **Additional “inducing another person” language (scope expansion):**  
   - IPC §389 (as quoted) covers fear/accusation of the person **having committed or attempted** the offence.

user_input: In the Indian criminal law framework, how does the treatment of “solitary confinement” by a sentencing court correspond between the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and what is one notable difference in how the rule is expressed across the two laws?
response:
Both laws give the sentencing court a **discretionary power** to impose **solitary confinement** only when the offence is one for which the court can sentence the convict to **rigorous imprisonment**, and they **cap the total solitary-confinement period at three months** following the same scale based on the length of imprisonment.

- Under **IPC §73**, the court may order solitary confinement for any portion(s) of the rigorous imprisonment **up to a total of three months**, applying this scale:  
  - up to **1 month** if imprisonment is **not more than 6 months**;  
  - up to **2 months** if imprisonment is **more than 6 months but not more than 1 year**;  
  - up to **3 months** if imprisonment is **more than 1 year**. **[2]**

- Under **BNS §11**, the court may likewise order solitary confinement for any portion(s) of the imprisonment **up to a total of three months**, with **the same scale** for durations. **[1]**

### One notable difference in expression
A key difference is **how the scale is written** in the second duration band:
- **IPC §73** includes the phrase **“shall not exceed one year”** for the middle bracket. **[2]**
- **BNS §11** states **“shall exceed six months and shall not exceed one year”** in the corresponding middle bracket—i.e., it repeats the full condition in the statutory text (a drafting/wording difference, though the practical threshold is the same). **[1]**
reference: Both the IPC and the BNS provide that, when sentencing for an offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment, the court may order solitary confinement for up to a total of three months, using the same tiered scale based on the length of the imprisonment (up to 1 month if up to 6 months; up to 2 months if more than 6 months up to 1 year; up to 3 months if more than 1 year). A notable difference is mainly drafting/wording: the BNS states the scale as separate clauses (a), (b), (c) and uses “namely,” while the IPC presents the same tiers in a continuous list and includes an internal bracketed wording artifact in the second tier.

### IPC (1860): putting someone in fear to facilitate extortion

Under the IPC, “fear” used to commit extortion appears in multiple sections, with different kinds of fear and different punishments:

1. **Fear of “any injury” (general fear)**
   - **IPC §385** criminalizes: *“in order to the committing of extortion, puts… in fear… of any injury”* (or attempts).
   - **Punishment:** imprisonment (either description) **up to 2 years**, **or** fine, **or both**.  
   - **Source:** [1]

2. **Fear of an “accusation of an offence” (specifically serious offences)**
   - **IPC §389** criminalizes putting/attempting to put someone in fear of an **accusation** of having committed or attempted to commit an offence punishable with:
     - **death** or **imprisonment for life** (or a form described as “imprisonment for life”), or
     - **imprisonment up to 10 years**.
     - (Also notes a special provision if the offence is punishable under **IPC §377**: may be punished with imprisonment for life.)
   - **Punishment:** imprisonment (either description) **up to 10 years**, **and** liable to fine.  
   - **Special outcome:** if the underlying offence is punishable under **IPC §377**, punishment *may* extend to imprisonment for life.  
   - **Source:** [2]

3. **Extortion via fear of death or grievous hurt**
   - **IPC §386** covers extortion **by putting** someone in fear of **death or grievous hurt** (to that person or any other).
   - **Punishment:** imprisonment (either description) **up to 10 years**, **and** liable to fine.  
   - **Source:** [3]

4. **Putting in fear of death/grievous hurt “in order to commit extortion” (attempted/anticipatory phrasing)**
   - **IPC §387** covers putting/attempting to put someone in fear of **death or grievous hurt** *“in order to the committing of extortion”* (to that person or any other).
   - **Punishment:** imprisonment (either description) **up to 7 years**, **and** fine.  
   - **Source:** [4]

---

### BNS (2023): putting someone in fear to facilitate extortion

The provided BNS excerpt directly states:

- **BNS §308(3)** criminalizes: *“in order to the committing of extortion, puts any person in fear, or attempts to put any person in fear, of any injury”*.
- **Punishment:** imprisonment (either description) **up to 2 years**, **or** fine, **or both**.
- **Source:** [5]

---

### Key comparison (wording, type of fear, and maximum punishment)

#### 1) **What “fear” is covered**
- **Fear of “any injury”**
  - **IPC §385**: fear of **any injury** to the person (or attempts). [1]
  - **BNS §308(3)**: same concept—fear of **any injury** (or attempts). [5]
  - **Effect:** Both laws clearly include a broad category: *any injury* (not limited to grievous hurt/death in these particular clauses).

- **Fear of “accusation of offence”**
  - **IPC §389** specifically covers fear of **accusation of an offence**, but only for **serious offences** (punishable with death/life or up to 10 years). [2]

- **Fear of death/grievous hurt**
  - **IPC §386** and **IPC §387** explicitly cover fear of **death or grievous hurt** (with different maximums). [3], [4]
  - **BNS:** In the provided BNS text, only **fear of “any injury”** is shown under §308(3); the excerpt does not separately specify “death or grievous hurt” categories. Therefore, from the CONTEXT, only the general “any injury” bucket is directly visible for BNS. [5]

#### 2) **Maximum imprisonment**
- For **fear of any injury**:
  - **IPC §385:** up to **2 years**. [1]
  - **BNS §308(3):** up to **2 years**. [5]
  - **So for this specific fear-type, maximum terms match.**

- For **fear of accusation/offence (IPC only, as per context):**
  - **IPC §389:** up to **10 years**. [2]

- For **fear of death/grievous hurt (IPC only, as per context):**
  - **IPC §386:** up to **10 years**. [3]
  - **IPC §387:** up to **7 years**. [4]

#### 3) **Availability of fine**
- **IPC §385:** fine is available (imprisonment up to 2 years, **or** fine, **or both**). [1]
- **BNS §308(3):** fine is available similarly (**or** fine, **or both**). [5]
- **IPC §386 / §387:** fine is expressly included (“**shall also be liable to fine**”). [3], [4]
- **IPC §389:** fine is expressly included (“**shall be liable to fine**”). [2]

---

### Bottom line
- **Both laws (as shown in the provided BNS clause and IPC §385) treat “putting in fear of any injury” to facilitate extortion as an offence punishable up to 2 years, with fine and/or imprisonment**. [1], [5]
- **IPC goes further in the provided sections** by separately addressing:
  - **fear of an accusation of a serious offence** (IPC §389, up to 10 years + fine), [2]
  - **fear of death or grievous hurt** (IPC §386 up to 10 years + fine; IPC §387 up to 7 years + fine). [3], [4]

The offence **“omission to give notice or information to a public servant by a person legally bound to give it”** in the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNS)** corresponds to **BNS §211**. [1]

**BNS §211** applies where a person, **legally bound** to give a notice or furnish information to a public servant, **intentionally omits** to do so **in the manner and at the time required by law**. [1]

## Punishment comparison with IPC version (IPC §176)
### IPC §176 (old law)
IPC §176 prescribes: [2]
- **General case:** simple imprisonment up to **1 month**, or fine up to **₹500**, or both; [2]  
- **If the notice/information relates to commission of an offence / prevention / apprehension of offender:** simple imprisonment up to **6 months**, or fine up to **₹1,000**, or both. [2]  
- (There is an additional bracketed/conditional part regarding an order under CrPC, 1898 s.565(1), with up to **6 months** and fine up to **₹1,000**.) [2]

### BNS §211 (new law)
BNS §211 prescribes: [1]
- **General case:** simple imprisonment up to **1 month**, or fine up to **₹5,000**, or both; [1]
- **If the notice/information relates to commission of an offence / prevention / apprehension of offender:** simple imprisonment up to **6 months**, or fine up to **₹10,000**, or both; [1]
- (Also includes a corresponding clause where required by an order under BNS s.394, with up to **6 months** and fine up to **₹1,000**, or both.) [1]

- **Same maximum imprisonment terms** as IPC §176: **1 month** (general) and **6 months** (serious-purpose cases). [1][2]

### One notable difference in punishment structure (especially when hurt is caused)
A key structural difference is that **BNS §109(1) expressly splits the “hurt is caused” punishment into a clear choice—*imprisonment for life* OR *up to 10 years + fine***, whereas the IPC framing (IPC §307) is more directly presented as **“either imprisonment for life or the punishment mentioned earlier”** within the same section text.

In BNS’s wording, this “hurt is caused” consequence is built more explicitly as an alternative:  
- **Life imprisonment** **or**  
- **the earlier capped term (up to 10 years) with fine**. [2]

(Also, BNS adds/clarifies an additional life-convict escalation rule under **§109(2)** when hurt is caused.) [2]
reference: The BNS provision for attempt to murder corresponds to the IPC offence of attempt to murder. A key difference is that the BNS expressly provides a maximum term of up to ten years (with fine) for the basic attempt, and separately states that if hurt is caused the offender may be punished with imprisonment for life or the earlier mentioned punishment; the IPC’s illustrations emphasize liability once the act is done toward murder, with punishment linked to whether hurt is caused.
